newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Falling Swedish CPI not seen affecting repo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Falling Swedish CPI not seen affecting repo.

text.p: Swedish prices fell for the fifth consecutive month in February but analysts said on Wednesday they doubted if the central bank, the Riksbank, would lower its key repo rate, in view of the soft crown.
"It was an incredibly strong figure, but I don't think it is enough for the Riksbank to lower the key repo rate," said James McKay, economist at PaineWebber.
"The Riksbank is also pressured by the soft crown," he said.
The crown had softened 44 percent to 4.4900 against the mark by Wednesday from 4.2995 about five months ago.

Swedish consumer price figures have repeatedly turned out lower than expected, beating analysts' forecasts. CPI fell 0.1 percent in February from January, while the market expected a 0.2 percent rise, according to a Reuter poll of 12 economists.
"During the past six months inflation has constantly been lower than forecasts. This is also the case this month." Nordbanken economist Olle Djerf said.
Nomura's Marco Pianelli said the discrepancies were because many underlying components were still weak.
The central bank has a target of 2.0 percent, with deviation of one percentage point on either side allowed.
The year-on-year February fall was 0.4 percent, giving Sweden disinflationary data for the fifth consecutive month. Prices were mainly depressed by lower mortgage costs.
EU-harmonised Swedish consumer prices, which do not include mortgage changes, were flat month-on-month and rose 1.1 percent year-on-year.
"As current interest rate costs are not in the net costs and the EU-harmonised CPI, this indicates very low total price increase levels," Djerf said.
"Inflation currently seems to be completely absent from the Swedish economy," he added.

But many analysts warned that the soft crown would stop the Riksbank making further cuts in its repo rate, which currently stands at 4.10 percent. It has not been moved so far in 1997, but was steadily cut throughout 1996 from 8.91 percent.
"I think the Riksbank wants to continue lowering the repo rate but that it is hampered by the soft crown," Ian Gunnar, economist at Chase Manhattan bank, said.
If the crown recovers, analysts say the bank could cut the repo when it makes a March 20 inflation report or soon after.
Sweden is not at all threatened by inflation, but analysts expect CPI to swing to positive figures shortly.

"The interest rate effect seems to be lasting longer than most had expected," John Eriksen, economist at I.D.E.A., said. "But it will disappear and the CPI will soon rise." --Stockholm newsroom +46 8 7001017
